<reason>Both sides argued tightly and narrowed the clash to the same population: students who obey the rule. B's strongest material (unenforceable bans, biased detectors, "disclosed vs hidden use") was largely neutralized when A conceded detectors and framed the ban as an authorship-based honor code, at which point B itself accepted that neither default catches the paster. That left the decisive question: what does each instruction produce in obedient students? A's answer—"told to write, the student writes; told to show prompts, the student annotates"—stayed live because B's rebuttal depended on reading "process transparency" as "process is the graded object," which A directly contested with the ordinary obedient case (generate, tidy, log "I checked") that the motion permits and B never showed would fail. B's fallback that interrogating the machine is itself the valuable skill is a real values clash, but B did less to weigh it against A's point that nightly homework is where composing is learned and occasional closed tasks can't replace it. B also had a clipped opening and mischaracterized [B1.7] as "unchallenged." A made the decision easier to render on the motion as written; B's rhetoric was excellent but its final frame ("preference not to know") slid past A's "knowing is not the good, practice is." Clear but competitive edge to A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 A2 [A4.3–A4.6]: distinguishing "process transparency" from "process is the graded object" and describing the ordinary obedient case (generate, tidy, log) that passes under the motion but is written under a ban—an attack on B's core "permissible to submit, not passable to grade" answer that B's closing never directly dismantled.</best_rebuttal>
